newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIA CARETAKER CABINET STARTS WORK ON CRISIS.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIA CARETAKER CABINET STARTS WORK ON CRISIS.

text.p: Bulgaria's caretaker cabinet takes office on Thursday, inheriting a grave economic crisis but also greater trust from Bulgarians and international lenders.
President Petar Stoyanov on Wednesday appointed a caretaker cabinet led by Sofia mayor Stefan Sofianski to govern until elections on April 19, and dissolved parliament with effect from February 19.
"Never have the Bulgarian people placed so much hope and expectation in a caretaker government," Stoyanov said at the swearing-in ceremony. Both he and Sofianski warned more hard times lay ahead.
"Fellow countrymen, I know the situation is grave but I cannot promise that in the next month the situation will become better," Stoyanov said in a televised address.

"Today our compatriots live in misery unknown to the civilised world. A misery which is not the result of people's inability to manage their destinies, but of the inability of those in power to provide better living conditions."

After 30 days of mass protests fuelled by economic hardship, the discredited Socialist majority last week gave up efforts to form a new cabinet and agreed to elections 20 months before the end of their parliamentary term.
Stoyanov said that in four years the Bulgarians had become 10 times poorer, the national currency had depreciated 100 times and domestic debt now topped three trillion levs.
Cumulative inflation from 1991 to end-1996 was 24,000 percent while wages in dollar terms had fallen seven times in the same period, he said.
Stoyanov, elected on the opposition ticket in November, won respect from all sides for breaking the political deadlock and brokering an agreement on early elections last week.

With the exception of a government of the opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) from November 1991 to December 1992, all Bulgaria's elected cabinets since 1989 have been led by or had the support of the ex-communist Socialist party.
"Once again we are back to where we started from: with inadequate prices and empty shelves. And again we are expecting yet another price shock," Stoyanov said.
Sofianski, 45, a leading UDF member, warned that escape from the crisis would require the efforts of every Bulgarian, not just the country's leaders.
"It is very important that during those months we put aside our small conflicts and mobilise all patience and decisiveness," he said.
He said the first big step had been taken with an all-party declaration on principles for the interim cabinet's handling of the crisis, signed by political leaders on Tuesday.

The International Monetary Fund, which suspended credits because of the Socialists' failure to carry out promised reforms, has said it will send a negotiating mission as soon as a caretaker cabinet is in place.
The presidency said the European Union would send an emergency mission in the next few days.
Parliament meets again on Thursday to clear outstanding legislation and to approve a bill authorising the caretaker cabinet to negotiate with international lenders.

Everything from bread to cigarettes and petrol is in short supply. Outgoing deputy transport minister Vasil Rangelov said one of the new cabinet's first tasks would be to secure fuel from state reserves to ensure key sectors keep functioning.

Police drove their vehicles in circles around the parliament and gathered outside the presidency on Wednesday to demand higher wages. Protests by army officers on Monday and Tuesday won a promise that their pay would be brought into line with other state salaries.
State carrier Balkan Airlines cancelled international flights for 24 hours for safety reasons after technical staff threatened pay strikes. Flights will resume on Thursday.

Still tougher times lie ahead for the government elected in April, which will have to sack thousands of employees in loss-making state firms and take the heat for severe budget restrictions accompanying a strict fixed exchange rate regime.
